findings.title: Unset of a personal key contradicts the collision remediation
findings.description:
Data Flow (line 89) says delete follows the key's scope, so `cf config unset git.integration_branch --project` removes the key only from `.context-forge.local.toml`. The collision case (line 146) and verification step 9 (line 259) nonetheless tell the user to run that same `unset` "to clear the stale shared-file copy." Step 9 also requires the personal file's value to remain untouched, which the same command would violate.

Actual result: the developer's confirmed personal value is deleted, the stale shared value becomes effective through the read fallback, and `cf check` still flags the shared copy. This is a silent wrong-value outcome in the one flow meant to repair it.

Fix: specify a remediation that actually clears the shared copy. For example, the migrate report prints the exact line to delete from `.context-forge.toml`, or a file-addressed clear is added. Then correct step 9 to match.

findings.title: Shared-file access is not defined by the ConfigManager contract
findings.description:
The API Contracts section says `get`/`set`/`delete`/`list` keep their signatures. None of them can address a single project file. `delete` routes by key scope, so it cannot remove a personal key's stale copy from the shared file. `list` merges both files.

Two new consumers need file-addressed access: `migrate-personal` (read and delete in the shared file) and the new ConsistencyChecker rule (enumerate keys in the shared file only). The design says to reuse the TOML helpers "as-is," but those helpers are not exported from the ConfigManager module. ConsistencyChecker receives its ConfigManager as an optional constructor dependency, and the design does not say what the rule does when it is absent.

Without a defined contract, implementers will duplicate file I/O outside ConfigManager or add a bypass that breaks the routing rule. Define the per-file read and delete methods (or a small file-store interface). State what the rule does without a ConfigManager: throw, or emit a finding. A silent skip would hide the warning.

findings.title: Read-path and per-key migration failures are not enumerated
findings.description:
The failure modes listed cover writes, the `.gitignore` append, and migrate's write-then-delete ordering. Three paths are missing:

1. Every project-scoped `get`/`list` now reads `.context-forge.local.toml`. A missing file is defined as empty. Malformed TOML and an unreadable file are not defined. The design should say they throw and surface, not fall back to empty.
2. The new shared-file scan has the same open question for an unparseable shared file.
3. `migrate-personal` "continues past a single key's failure," which means catching per-key errors. The project's exception rules permit only: re-raise after `logger.exception` at ERROR; a specific exception swallowed with a stated reason; or a process-boundary handler. The design should name which applies and require an ERROR-level log in addition to the report line.

findings.title: Existing projects do not get the personal file ignored
findings.description:
Technical Scope says `cf init` and `cf check` must give enough awareness to keep personal settings out of git. The Value section (line 23) says the goal is to prevent them from being silently committed.

`cf init` is the only path that adds the `.gitignore` line. A project initialized before this slice gets the line only if the user re-runs init, and nothing prompts that. Once this ships, the first `cf config set git.integration_branch ... --project` creates an un-ignored `.context-forge.local.toml` in exactly those projects, which is the leak this slice exists to stop. The new `cf check` rule covers only personal keys inside the shared file, not missing ignore coverage.

Recommendation: add an explicit `cf check` warning when `.context-forge.local.toml` exists and is not ignored, naming the file. This surfaces the gap rather than silently editing `.gitignore` on write.

findings.title: Migration machinery is heavier than the one-key case needs
findings.description:
Only one key is personal today: `git.integration_branch` (line 111). The migration command still carries per-key processing, per-key failure isolation, and a `failed:` report state. The command is one-time and idempotent, so the failure isolation can be cut: process the key, abort on the first error, and rerun.

Keep the collision rules. Skipping a differing personal value and deleting an identical shared copy protect data. Cut the "continue past a single key's failure" behavior.

The Verification Walkthrough (lines 225–259) also restates the Functional Requirements (lines 212–218) in longer form. Keep one of the two.

findings.title: Precedence adds a layer rather than reusing the existing pattern
findings.description:
The plan asks to reuse the existing user-vs-project merge pattern rather than invent one. The design adds a third project-level tier, a special case where personal keys fall back to the shared file, and a new `source` value.

The fallback is justified by migration, and it is surfaced (`source: project` plus the check), so it is not silent. Record it explicitly as a deliberate exception to the generic merge. Step 2 of the read flow (lines 77–81) is also hard to follow: both branches end at "check the shared file." Rewrite it as one rule: after a personal miss, or for a shared key, check the shared file.

findings.title: Plan entry and design disagree on dependencies
findings.description:
The frontmatter lists `dependencies: [914]`, and Prerequisites require 914 and the 916 scope fix. Plan entry 915 says "Dependencies: none." The plan's 916 entry (guide-update branch guard) does not mention the `--project` scope prerequisite. That prerequisite is documented only in the 916 slice doc's Prerequisite Fix section.

Both prerequisites are complete, so there is no execution risk. The plan entry should still record them.

findings.title: Worktree resolution of the personal value is not stated
findings.description:
The rationale says the personal value is per-developer and per-worktree. The project's Git Rules section says `cf worktree init` gives each worktree its own `git.integration_branch`.

The design does not say whether each worktree's personal file is its own root's `.context-forge.local.toml`, or how `cf worktree` set/get reach ConfigManager. The worktree command source does not reference ConfigManager directly; its CLI tests mock it. Confirm the routing and state the expected per-worktree file location in the design.
